The *Miaoxuan* (Exquisite Profundity) demonstrates how the Bodhisattva transcends and severs residual habit-energies (vāsanā).

(28) Entering the provisional from emptiness, the contemplation of the Path and the contemplation of phenomena flow together; one deeply contemplates the two truths and advances to sever residual habit-energies, wherein both matter and mind are devoid of [independent] cognition.

One attains the Dharma-eye and the knowledge of the modes of the path (mārgajñatā). (And so forth. One studies the ten powers (daśabala) and four fearlessnesses (caturvaiśāradya) of a Buddha; the habitual tendencies (vāsanā) are nearly exhausted.

*Miaoxuan* (The Profound Meaning), fascicle 4, section on the Buddha-ground of the Shared Teaching (sāmānyayāna), clarifying that one achieves the Way by sustaining the habitual tendencies; *Qian* (Commentary), fascicle 5, section 21.

Having transcended the stages of a bodhisattva, one enters the stage of a Buddha. By means of his vows, he sustains residual habits (*vāsanā*) and is born in Jambudvīpa, accomplishing the Way through the eight manifestations.

(The commentary below the passage "having transcended the stages of a bodhisattva" explains the stage of a Buddha; the *Jizuan* [Sub-commentary], fascicle 4, states: "Because during his time as a bodhisattva he retained residual habits to moisten his rebirth, when he reached the foot of the Bodhi tree, he merely severed those remaining habits.")

The *Shiqian* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning) clarifies that the five [aspects] of the Immovable Samādhi (IX) and the four (XIII) of the *Xuanyu* concern the retribution and the three delusions (*san-huo*). Regarding the formation of the "three immovables" (*san-budong*): "movement" (*dong*) here includes karma (*ye*). Since there are only three truths (*di*), karma along with the afflictions of views (*jian*) and thought (*si*) are included together because they are equally sublated within the conventional truth (*suodi*). [Answer]: It is because these [afflictions] are what obstruct the attainment of the ultimate truth. Furthermore, the ultimate truth is not something to be attained; rather, it is the very state of non-attainment. Therefore, the ultimate truth does not involve the sublation of anything. Consequently, the term "ultimate truth" is used here merely as a provisional designation for the conventional truth. What, among these, is that which is subverted by conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*)? Dharmajñāna answers: "In this context, karma and the afflictions of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) likewise enter into the conventional truth of birth-and-death; they are precisely what is subverted by ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), thereby accomplishing the samādhi of ultimate truth.

As for the remaining text, which states that karma is subverted by the sands of dust [of phenomena] to accomplish the samādhi of conventional truth, each has its own underlying reason. Why is this? Just as in the preceding passages on the "Stainless" (*vimala*) and others, where mundane wholesome roots (*prākṛta-kuśala*) subvert evil karma—mundane wholesome roots constitute the contemplation of the provisional (*upāya-vipaśyanā*)—here, it is by means of fixed wholesome roots (*niyata-kuśala*) that one subverts mundane wholesome roots, thereby accomplishing the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).

Therefore, it is said that "the renunciations (*pratyāhāra*) suppress the afflictions of view and thought. The Master of the Commentary (Jiji) has exhausted the profound mysteries, and thus provides this correspondence.
24. *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy) explains that in the Hīnayāna, the two types of non-cognition (*ajñāna*) are identical in essence.

Specifically, within the Hīnayāna, obscured non-cognition (*kliṣṭājñāna*) has ignorance (*avidyā*) as its essence, while unobscured non-cognition (*akliṣṭājñāna*) has inferior wisdom (*hīnaprajñā*) as its essence.
This refers to [the lack of knowledge regarding] taste, potency, maturation, qualities, number, time, and measure.

The *Myōryaku* (Wondrous Joy) states that Śāriputra, in the sixth stage (*bhūmi*) of the Separate Teaching (*bypō*), severed both the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and the delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*), being thus a worldling (*pṛthagjana*).

(The *Fuxing* [Sub-commentary], fascicle 2, says: "Because he destroyed the delusions of views, he departed from the four evil destinies; because he destroyed the delusions of thought, he departed from birth within the triple realm.

Regarding the sixteenth [stage], according to the intent of the *Yíngluò* (Jewel Garland), Śāriputra regressed at the sixth mind within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*); it is likely that this refers to the period prior to that, when both the delusions of views and thought were still present.

Both are severed. By the time of the sixth mind, however, the [delusions of] views (*dṛṣṭi*) are not yet exhausted; one may still regress from the sixth mind [to become] an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). [Japanese Question: Modern skeptics ask:

"In the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavahāra*), it is said that at the first *vihāra* (stage), the delusions of view within the realm of desire are already completely severed. How could it be that at the sixth *vihāra*, the delusions of view are still not exhausted, such that one regresses to become an ordinary person who commits the heinous crimes (*ānantarya-karma*)? [Answer of Fazhi:

Regarding the standard course of the Separate Teaching, it is generally said that at the first *vihāra* one severs the delusions of view and will no longer give rise to various grave transgressions. Furthermore, although the categories of the delusions of view are numerous, they are all severed instantaneously in a single stage. The delusions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), however, are only exhausted after passing through various stages. This is the constant discourse regarding the boundaries of the Separate Teaching. Now, the Master of the Record (Jizang) observes that Śāriputra [fell back] at the sixth...

Even while abiding [in the stage of non-retrogression], one may still regress and further commit grave offenses. Thus, seeking the matter through principle, one fears there may be scriptural evidence that both the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi*) and thought (*citta*) are severed simultaneously; yet, by the time of the sixth mental moment, the delusions of thought are not yet exhausted, and the delusions of views remain as a residue. This is why one can still be dragged into the evil realms. These words are the Master of the Commentary’s own deliberations based on the underlying meaning.

Below, one may raise the difficulty using the *pratyutpanna* (manifest) distinct teaching (*biejiao*). According to the *Qixin lun*, it is said that only those who have attained non-retrogression are capable [of such progress]. However, when distinguishing this from the perspective of a person of the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*), even when discussing the manifestation of traces, one must also manifest their respective stages;
it is only when categorized according to the limits of their afflictions (*kleśa*) that the possibility of regression exists.
The *Myōryaku* (Wondrous Joy) explains that both types of the three realms possess the factors of view-delusion (*dṛṣṭi*) and thought-delusion (*saṃjñā*).
[Section 9] (38). [Section 9] (30).
These are simply the two deaths and the five abodes (*pañca-vihāra*). One should know that the name "three realms" is pervasive; it applies both within and outside the realms. If the realm...

The reason for establishing the names of the three realms externally is that the external corresponds to the internal. Since the underlying principle has not yet been fully exhausted, they are collectively termed "delusions of view" (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), which pervade all three realms.
Within the *parināmika* (transformation) lands, the five sublime sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) are called the "desire-realm delusions of view and thought" (*kāmadhātu-dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*).
The inconceivable mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) are called the "thought-delusions of the upper realms."
The names, phrases, and sentences of the Lotus Sutra clarify that Bodhisattvas sustain their residual habits through the seventeen (eighteen) vows,
entering into birth and death while not taking emptiness as a final realization.

In the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*), within the explanation of the *nirodhasatya* (truth of cessation) of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*), there is a section refuting the "dust-like" [delusions] (*pāṃśu-saṃkhyeya*).

First (13), second (9): regarding "dust-like," it is a metaphor for the vast number of instances of ignorance. Other interpretations hold that there are only two types: first, defiled; second, non-defiled. Non-defiled refers to habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
The intention of our school (*jījiā*) is that the habitual tendencies of the Hīnayāna are precisely the delusions specific to the Separate Teaching; therefore, we now explain them by dividing them.
The sixteen gates, both internal and external to the realms, consist of knowing the illness, identifying the medicine, and administering the medicine.
Regarding the three types—corresponding, independent, and mixed—within the internal realms (21):

if one is deluded regarding the provisional principle, there arise the ignorance associated with the internal realms, whether corresponding or independent, along with the various proclivities (*anuśaya*) of views and afflictions.
That which is combined is called "associated" (*saṃprayukta*); that which is not associated is called "independent" (*mūla*).
In the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), explaining the twenty-fifth [topic], it says:

regarding "independent," the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "It is non-common ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*), which does not coexist with the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*). It further asks: "Is it also non-common restlessness (*auddhatya*)?"
[Question: Are there [afflictions] such as the *paryavasthānas*? [Answer: No.

Regarding the three types—associated with the supramundane (*lokottara*), independent (*svatantra*), and both—of ignorance (*avidyā*) within the realm of clarity (*vidyā-dhātu*) of śamatha and vipaśyanā:
if one is deluded regarding the true principle (*tattva-artha*), then there exists associated and independent ignorance pertaining to the supramundane. Why is this so? Because the realm...

Although within the internal [consciousness] the associated and independent [afflictions] have been severed, the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) still remain. In the Hīnayāna, these tendencies are not considered primary afflictions (*kleśa*);
however, according to the definitive teaching of the Mahāyāna, the tendencies are themselves distinct afflictions—namely, the ignorance (*avidyā*) that exists beyond the realms (*dhātu*).

The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) explains that although there are both associated (*samyukta*) and independent (*svatantra*) [afflictions] outside the realms (*dhātu*), they differ fundamentally from those within the realms; specifically, they obstruct the Middle Way.
Those that are associated (*saṃprayukta*) and also conjoined with the various proclivities (*anuśaya*) of views and afflictions outside the realms are called "associated.
Those that directly obstruct the principle are called "independent" (*muktaka*). Regarding what is called "associated," it is as when it is said: "From this point onward, all are termed wrong view.

Furthermore, from the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) onwards, one cultivates the dhyāna that is free from views; this refers to the identical-substance view (*tongti-jian*) outside the realms. This is the preparatory stage (*upāya*).

The five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) of the two lands of True Reward (*sahaja-vipāka*) constitute the "delusions of thought" (*vitarka-kleśa*) outside the [three] realms. Such views and thoughts necessarily involve ignorance (*avidyā*), which is termed "associated.

The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) indicates that although the *kleśas* of dust-like delusions (*rajas-kleśa*) do not pull one toward karmic retribution, they must nonetheless be severed first before one can advance to cultivate the Middle Way.
[Question] (27) Regarding the doubt:
"Moistening birth outside the realm is precisely due to ignorance (*avidyā*). Since it is not due to the *pāṃśu-saṃudghāta* [obstructions], why must it be severed first?

[Answer] The commentary states: Because it obstructs the path of transformation (*nirmāṇa-mārga*), it must be severed first. It is severed first because it serves as the skillful means (*upāya*) for true transformation. Severed.

Only then can one advance to cultivate Madhyamaka. This destroys the real retribution, the corresponding [afflictions], and the independent [afflictions]. The *dharmas* as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are the branches;
ignorance is the root.
[The four types of] craving and views regarding the three truths are present in both *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. (16) [End of] Record 4, Part 1.

The "three robes" refer to the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*). They conceal the blemishes upon the three truths and shield one from the cold and heat of views and craving within the three truths (for each truth possesses both craving and views; craving is like heat, and views are like cold).
The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) quotes the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* regarding the phrase "vowing to support residual habits" (*shì fúxí*) which gives rise to the five lower [realms] (24).
As for "vowing to support residual habits," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "One retains the remaining residual habits; by the power of one's vow, one then supports those residual habits."
Thus, one is born into the three realms to bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings.
Regarding "cessation and contemplation" (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*), they are named after their function of resolving delusions of view;

(33) however, since "view" (*darśana*) refers to seeing the principle, and seeing reality is not itself a delusion—it is at the moment of seeing the principle that this delusion is severed—they are nonetheless named after the resolution [of the delusion].
It is simply called "afflictions of view.
When correctly contemplating and resolving these afflictions of view, they receive their designation according to their essential nature (v. 34).

Furthermore, the afflictions of view do not merely receive their name according to how they are resolved; they also receive their designation according to their essential nature. They are termed "provisional" (prajñapti), for they are provisional.
This refers to that which is false, illusory, and inverted; it is merely designated by the name "provisional" (*prajñapti*).
In the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), fascicle 5, part 2 (13), it is explained that the essence itself is called "view.
A view is nothing but the provisional. To be provisional means simply to be unreal in its meaning. Although the names obtained differ, [the underlying principle remains the same].

The substance of "seeing" (dṛṣṭi) is not distinct [from that of "wisdom"]. The reason for emphasizing that the substance itself is designated by provisional names (*prajñapti*) is the desire to establish the meaning of the three types of provisional designations (*tri-prajñapti*) for each and every instance, so that one may know that the substance of seeing is itself provisional.
Therefore, it was previously stated: "The substance of seeing is provisional. "Provisional" refers here to the three types of provisional designations.

Furthermore, the preceding text states: "It receives its name from understanding; only when one realizes the principle (*tattva*) is [the affliction] severed. Why, then, must the realization of the principle necessarily involve the inference of the three types of provisional designations? This is [the question].

Therefore, it is further stated that names are provisional based on their very substance (*tattva*). One should refute the provisional through the four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*). Since the provisional is refuted, one perceives the principle (*tattva*).
Furthermore, it should also be stated that [the provisional] gives rise to delusions.
Regarding the vertical penetration of the dharma through both arising and non-arising in the context of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, there are five [sections]:
(46) and five below (27).

Is this the case where non-arising is practiced and true arising occurs? Or is it the case where the non-arising of the sands of phenomena universally accords with arising? (That which "universally accords with arising" refers to the subversion of the one...)

Upon severing the first delusion, one immediately attains immeasurable worldly-truth samādhis (laukika-satya-samādhi), whereby one acts with sovereign mastery for the benefit of beings; this is called "Universal Function Arising" (*tongyong sheng*).
Regarding the cessation and contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) that liberates one from the delusions of thought (*jiewu*), they derive their name from liberation.
First, when contemplating the truth, it is still shallow and there remain obstacles of conditioned phenomena (*saviṣaya-āvaraṇa*); subsequently, one repeatedly deliberates upon the truth.
These delusions are thereby eliminated; thus, they are called "delusions of contemplation" (*sī-vyā-kleśa*).

In the *Śraddhā-bhūmi* (Stages of Faith) of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, it is clarified that in the Perfect Teaching, from the eighth to the tenth faith, the habitual tendencies of these delusions of contemplation are completely severed.
(Recorded in Volume Six, Part Eight; Upper Volume, Part Nine).

The *Avataṃsaka* states: "At the moment of first generating the mind [of enlightenment], the fundamental afflictions (*āsrava*) and their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are simultaneously exhausted without remainder.

This refers to the exhaustion of fundamental afflictions and habitual tendencies within the realm; it does not mean that the fundamental afflictions and habitual tendencies outside the realm have been exhausted. (As for the claim that the habitual tendencies are exhausted from the eighth stage of faith through the tenth, this is because "habitual tendencies" here refers generally to all the dust-like ignorance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) that exist externally.)

The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*) clarifies, both according to the literal text and according to the underlying meaning, that view-delusion (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), thought-delusion (*saṃjñā-kleśa*), and ignorance (*avidyā*) constitute the six lower [stages].

(7) If explained according to the text, view-delusion and thought-delusion obstruct the True [Dharma], while ignorance obstructs the Middle. If explained according to the underlying meaning, there is no separate ignorance apart from view-delusion and thought-delusion;

since the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of ignorance is identical to the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), one should know that view-delusion and thought-delusion are likewise identical to the Dharma-nature.

(The subsequent text further states: "How could there be dust-like afflictions outside of the delusions of views and thoughts? How could there be ignorance after the two contemplations? Since the three delusions are identical, the three contemplations must be fused.")
The profound revelation of *nirvāṇa* concerns the residual habits (*vāsanā*) of both the views and the afflictions (*kleśa*).

(8) The "lesser" refers to the followers of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*). Although they have severed the afflictions, they still possess residual habits, such as thinking "I am the body," "this is my robe," "I go," or "I come.
They regard the Buddha as equal to themselves, maintaining that there is only permanence and purity, and no self, pleasure, or [purity]. This constitutes the distinction of the Three Jewels.
Because of their residual habits (*vāsanā*), they are considered "small.

The *Weimo xuanshu* (Profound Commentary on the Vimalakīrti) clarifies that according to the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*), at the time of sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) like a Buddha, one severs all residual habits. (16)

"Wisdom corresponding to a single thought-moment that exhausts all habitual tendencies" refers to the habitual tendencies of the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the obstructions to the knowable (*dharmāvaraṇa*).

(The subsequent text further states: "In the Shared Teaching (*pāryāyika-yāna*), one progressively abandons the habitual tendencies as well as the non-cognition regarding form and mind, thereby attaining the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgajñatā*").)

The *Weimo xuanshu* (Profound Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra), citing the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, clarifies that the afflictions of craving within the three realms of transformation are [overcome by] the three great wisdoms.
The *Dazhidu lun* explains that when Kāśyapa heard the sound of the *ciṅkāra* lute, he could not remain at ease.
Kāśyapa said, "I have already severed the five desires of the three realms. This is because these are the five desires produced from the pure and wondrous merit of a bodhisattva.
Regarding this matter, one cannot find peace within oneself. This applies equally to the cravings of the form and formless realms.

In the *Weimo xuanshu* (Profound Commentary on the Vimalakīrti), the "Purity" and "Stainlessness" of Vimalakīrti are explained through the categories of distinct afflictions (*biehuo*), fundamental afflictions (*zheng*), and residual habits (*xi*).

Since Vimalakīrti is a Great Being (*mahāsattva*) in his final birth before Buddhahood (*isheng bushu*), he is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), abiding at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*dingjue*) with the diamond-like mind (*vajracitta*).
This is the stage of the Bodhisattva Vimala. Because the principle of Buddha-nature is manifest, it is called "Pure.

Since both the primary delusions and their habitual tendencies are completely exhausted, and the residual traces of ignorance are like a wisp of smoke—existing yet as if non-existent—it is therefore called "Stainless" (Vimala).

The *Vimalakīrti-vyākhyā* clarifies that through the correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*) of the Middle Way, one severs the residual habits (*vāsanā*) and destroys the two extremes of the real and the conventional.

Upon reaching the ultimate limit of the *Vajraśekhara*, when wisdom is perfected and the essence of the Middle Way is manifested, the three delusions are finally exhausted, leaving no further residual habits. In the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), this begins from the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) and continues through to the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmamegha*).
He has completely severed all views, yet residual habits (*vāsanā*) still remain. Upon attaining Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), he enters the profound mystery;

for thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, he further cultivates all mundane affairs until his realization of principle is distinct and his residual habits are attenuated, such that these affairs are like a wisp of smoke.

Therefore, it is said that he is "without further residual habits. It is like throwing a small amount of salt into a great river; it no longer possesses a salty taste. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The two views of existence and non-existence are extinguished."
There is nothing further. The true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is what the Buddha taught; yet, [some] merely claim that one severs the two views within the realm of desire.

Furthermore, according to the specific interpretation of the *Dilun* school, upon ascending to the stages (*bhūmi*), one leaves behind the obstacles of the ordinary person’s mark of self and severs the views of existence and non-existence.

How could this possibly account for the meaning of this sūtra passage? Question: What fault is there in this? Answer: In the *Zang* (Āgama) and *Tong* (Shared) teachings, the various views are severed at the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). In the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*), they are severed upon ascending to the stages.

One severs the views outside the realm of cessation (*nirodhadhātu*). Furthermore, one must not fail to extol the virtues of the stage of "near-enlightenment" (*upapatti-bhūmi*). The *Upāsaka-sūtra* states: "In the ninth stage, one severs the habit-energies of views;
in the tenth stage, one severs the habit-energies of craving. The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states: "The pure dhyāna that is free from all views.

This refers to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Therefore, we now rely upon this to interpret the present text. In this way, the meaning of the "perfect severance" (*yuan-duan*) according to our school becomes even more distinct.
The *Vimalakīrti-vyākhyā* quotes from the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* regarding the "Gate of Entering the Double Profundity" (2).
As for the "Gate of Entering the Double Profundity," the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states: "Regarding the power of entering, abiding, and arising in dhyāna: one again enters the dhyāna of power.

'Entering' means entering all dharma-gates from the ordinary mind up to the arising from the higher stages. 'Power' means arising from the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi-bhūmi*) and entering [the ultimate]."
Regarding "all dharma-gates": one who dwells [in them] dwells according to all dharma-gates, which is to say, they dwell within all dharma-gates.
Regarding "returning to enter [them] again": this refers to practicing them anew for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas.

In the *Vimalakīrti-vyākhyā-saṃkṣepa*, regarding the explanation of the three obstacles to the Dharma (*dharmāvaraṇa*), the pervasive delusions (*paryavasthāna-kleśa*), and the primary and residual habits (*mūla-vāsanā*);
and concerning the two wisdoms of the provisional and the real (*prajñā*) of the Tripiṭaka Master [Xuanzang]: (15) Upper Part, Section Two (Yù 46).

The wisdom of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is ultimately clear and distinct; when all obstacles to the Dharma are exhausted, it is termed the "wisdom of provisional means in one's own practice" (*svayaṃ-caryā-upāya-jñāna*). The principle of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is thoroughly investigated...

Ultimately clear and distinct; when both the fundamental afflictions and their habitual tendencies are exhausted, it is called "true wisdom" (the "dharma-obstructions" refer to the *dhūli-saṃsāra* [dust-like] defilements within the realm).
In the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā*, it is clarified that Bodhisattvas are not moved by the five desires outside the realm.
(21) That the flowers fall upon the Bodhisattvas signifies that the Bodhisattvas abide in the inconceivable liberation and give rise to the true retribution (*vipāka*).

The earth. Having already separated from and departed from delusions, he cannot be moved by those exquisite five desires; therefore, flowers do not adhere to his body, but all fall away of their own accord.
The *Vimalakīrti-vyākhyā* directly takes "separated delusions" (*bie-huo*) to mean the residual habits (*vāsanā*) of the Hīnayāna. (21)
The followers of the Two Vehicles have only severed the five desires within the realm; therefore, they cannot be moved by the five worldly desires.

However, because their secondary afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) have not been eliminated, they are defiled by the exquisite forms and sounds beyond the realm. Thus, it is said in reproach: "If the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the fetters are not yet exhausted, flowers will cling to the body.
This is like the story in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* where Kāśyapa, upon hearing the *kiṃnara* lute, could not remain composed and immediately remarked: [as follows].
The winds from the eight directions cannot move Mount Sumeru; yet when the *sūlana* wind arrives, it shatters [the mountain] like rotten grass.
As for the five desires of the three realms, I have already severed them completely; they cannot move my mind. This is what is meant by "these are the pure and wondrous five desires of a Bodhisattva.
That I cannot find peace in these matters is precisely the meaning of that statement.
In the *Vimalakīrti-vyākhyā*, based on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the small vehicle (*hīnayāna*) distinguishes afflictions (*kleśa*) from their residual impressions (*vāsanā*).

(22) Question: This sutra states that if residual habits (*saṃyojana-vāsanā*) are not yet exhausted, flowers will adhere to the body. How does this relate to distinct afflictions? Answer: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "Regarding..."

In the Śrāvaka sūtras, these are called *vāsanā* (habitual tendencies); in the Mahāyāna, they are called *mūlakleśa* (root afflictions), which refers specifically to the secondary delusions (*pṛthag-moha*).
Regarding why the *Vimalakīrti-sūtra-ṭīkā* distinguishes these secondary delusions as being termed the "four abodes" (*catur-vāsabhūmi*) or not, there are eight points. (Question 22):

Do both the universal delusions (*sāmānya-kleśa*) and the secondary delusions (*pṛthag-kleśa*) receive the name "four abodes"? (Answer): If one speaks in terms of the internal realms of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-śāsana*), [both are so designated].

Regarding the names of the four abidings (*catur-vāsa*): if one connects the distinct teaching (*bhedavyavahāra*) with the shared teaching (*sāmānyavyavahāra*), then outside the realms there is only the name "ignorance" (*avidyā*).

Ignorance can obstruct the Buddha-nature and is not termed "view-delusion" (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) or "thought-delusion" (*bhava-kleśa*). If one relies on the distinct teaching, ignorance is itself the fundamental afflictions (*mūlakleśa*), and it also possesses the names of the four abidings of view-delusion and thought-delusion.
Therefore, the heavenly maiden rebuked him, saying: "If one makes distinctions regarding the Buddha-dharma, that is not [in accordance with]..."

The Dharma involves conceptual discrimination; thus, it constitutes the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). Furthermore, it is said that because the compilation [of the teachings] was not yet complete, the flowers remained attached to his body;
therefore, there were the delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*). These can also be categorized as three stages of dwelling (*trivihāra*).
The Commentary on the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa, Clarifying the Characteristics of Delusions of Perception Beyond the Realm (8), Part 22:
Those of the Two Vehicles loathe the five desires of the world and seek *nirvāṇa*. This indicates that their minds harbor attachment and aversion.

Now, when they see the five desires as the karmic reward of a Bodhisattva, they likewise deem them improper; yet though they abandon, reject, and push them away, they cannot depart from them. (Thus it is said.)
It is said: "The heavens respond with a non-discriminating mind and disperse [the flowers] with a non-discriminating mind.
Because the Bodhisattvas possess a non-discriminating mind, the flowers do not adhere to them. Śāriputra and others discriminate between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa as being different;
such discrimination is precisely the delusion of views."

The *Vimalakīrti-sūtra-ṭīkā*: Distinguishing between Shared and Unshared Habitual Tendencies (23). Question: Is this definitely an unsevered distinct fetter (*pṛthag-bandhana*), or is it the habitual tendency (*vāsanā*) of a common fetter?
Answer: If categorized according to the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*), such as in the case of Kāśyapa, it is a habitual tendency.

If categorized according to the Distinct Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*), it is because a distinct fetter has not yet been severed that there is a habitual tendency; as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
Explanation: There are two kinds of fetters (*saṃyojana*): first, those severed by the Two Vehicles; second, those not shared with the Two Vehicles.
Those shared [with the Two Vehicles] have already been severed by Kāśyapa; those not shared [with the Two Vehicles] have not yet been severed by Kāśyapa, as explained above.
Since this sutra now clarifies the inconceivable liberation (*acintya-vimokṣa*), it specifically employs the severance of the Distinct and Perfect [Teachings].

The *Guangming wenju* (Text on the Words of Light), citing the *Dichi jing* (Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra), states: "In the tenth [stage], regarding the ninth 'Pure-Purity Dhyāna' (*viśuddha-viśuddha-dhyāna*), all afflictions—whether general or specific, whether manifest or latent—are completely exhausted. (Record 1, Section 19).
If one enters the ninth "Pure-Purity Dhyāna," all afflictions, both general and specific, whether active or habitual, are entirely extinguished.

As for this ninth dhyāna, one immediately proceeds from the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and enters into wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Therefore, it is said that all delusions—both universal and particular, as well as their active outbursts (*maula-kleśa*) and residual habits (*vāsanā*)—are completely exhausted. From the tenth stage downward, there remain both active outbursts and residual habits. In the *Huayan jing lun* (Treatise on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra), the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samalaṃbuddhi*) is not distinguished from the ten stages;

it is, in fact, identical to them. When it is stated that universal and particular delusions, along with their active outbursts and residual habits, are all exhausted: "universal" refers to the four abodes (*catur-vāsabhūmi*), and "particular" refers to ignorance (*avidyā*). Regarding universal delusions, the active outbursts are exhausted at the seventh level of faith (*śraddhā*) in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*); the residual habits continue until Buddhahood. As for particular delusions, both the active outbursts and residual habits are exhausted [at the stage of Equal Enlightenment]. Thus, because...

Now, regarding the household [tradition] concerning the latencies (*vāsanā*) of the Hīnayāna: because they differentiate sixteen gates (four sets of four), if one speaks of the separate afflictions (*pṛthag-kleśa*), there are forty-two grades, and the stages of their abandonment are as usual. As for the latencies, they are explained only as stated in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā*.

That text cites the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, stating that because it is "separated from all views" and is "pure, pure dhyāna," it clarifies only the latency of views. If one cites the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra*, which states that the tenth stage abandons the latency of craving—the tenth stage being equivalent to Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-sambodhi*)—how could this not enter the "Twofold Profundity" (*chóngxuán*)?

Therefore, we know that while the separate afflictions abandon the fundamental propensities (*mūla-anuśaya*), the external propensities enter the Twofold Profundity to abandon the latencies; the text is very clear on this point.
In the *Guangming wenju* (Exegesis on the Words of Light), regarding the section "The Buddha’s Severing of the Bonds of Views, Exhausting Both the Common and the Particular" (31):
that which is severed by the Two Vehicles is the common bond of views; that which is severed by the Bodhisattvas is the particular bond of views. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:

"If the habitual tendencies of the fetters are not yet exhausted, flowers will cling to the body. This means that because the particular bonds of views have not been severed, one is beset by flowers. Yet it is said that [this occurs] for the Buddha...

Regarding the fetters of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*): although it is said that Bodhisattvas are able to sever individual views, they have not yet severed them completely; their ultimate severance occurs only with the Buddha. If one reaches the stage of Buddhahood, [they are fully severed].

[Commentary on the Four Truths (26)] Although it is said that Bodhisattvas can sever individual views, they have not yet severed them exhaustively; the ultimate [severance] resides in the Buddha. If one reaches the stage of Buddhahood...
It is not only the distinct [delusions] that are exhausted; the universal [delusions] are likewise brought to their ultimate limit. Why is this?

If [the delusions] arise from the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) of sentient beings throughout the six realms across the ten directions—those accomplished through various seeds and habitual tendencies—they are severed at the stage of the causal ground (*hetu-bhūmi*), yet their boundaries are not yet fully exhausted.

Only the Buddha reaches the ultimate consummation. Therefore, it is said: "Whether universal or distinct, the ultimate consummation lies with the Buddha. (The *Suo yin ji*, fascicle 1, states: "Universal refers to the views and afflictions; distinct refers to the dust-like afflictions (*rajas-kleśa*); and ignorance [*avidyā*]...")

There are both general and specific [aspects] for each. Having thoroughly exhausted the general through correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*), one looks back longingly to what preceded it. The record states: "The ear-door is exhausted of delusion; how are the specific afflictions (*bhinna-kleśa*) and their residual habits (*vāsanā*) distinguished? Answer: Since there is no distinct essence between the views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana* and *vitarka-vicāra*) outside the realms (*dhātu-bāhya*), how could the residual habits of the fundamental afflictions (*mūla-kleśa*) possibly be two different things?
Regarding the four foundations of mindfulness (*catur-smṛtyupasthāna*), there are three meanings concerning the realization of principle (*tattva*) by the three vehicles.

First, there are three types: (1) for the Śrāvaka, it is said that principle exists outside of the active afflictions (*paryavasthāna*); (2) for the Pratyekabuddha, it is said that principle exists outside of the latent tendencies (*vāsanā*);

(3) for the Bodhisattva, it is said that principle exists outside of both the active afflictions and the latent tendencies. These three persons must see the principle only after [transcending] these three types of externality; therefore, it is said that "principle is threefold."

Regarding the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*), there are two types of practitioners [the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas] who sever the fetters both collectively and individually.
(12) When the wisdom that severs the fetters collectively is coarse, one merely eliminates the active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*); such a person is called a Śrāvaka.
If the wisdom of individual characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) is subtle, it penetrates the latent tendencies (*vāsanā*); such a person is called a Pratyekabuddha.
The four foundations of mindfulness demonstrate the characteristics of the delusions of the three realms outside the [true] realm.

(1) If one were to explain these separately as being outside the realm: upon attaining the stages (*bhūmi*), one abandons the distinct views; from the second stage through the sixth stage, one abandons the distinct afflictions of desire-realm thought;
and at the seventh stage, one abandons the distinct afflictions of the form and formless realms. This, too, is merely the sense of partial abandonment. (And so forth.)

The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* explains that at the beginning of the Immaculate Ground (*vimalā-bhūmi*) of Equal Enlightenment, one first attains liberation from views and enters the meditative concentration of pure vision.

One should know that this marks the departure from the afflictions of the desire realm, as well as those of the form and formless realms; it is only upon reaching Equal Enlightenment that these are completely exhausted, which constitutes the meaning of "perfection" (*pariniṣpanna*).
If it were the case that one only begins to depart from the retributive fruits of the formless realm at the eighth ground, that would be the meaning of partial severance.
In the *Guanyin xuanyi*, the commentary on "the thirty-four minds where both the fundamental afflictions (*zheng*) and habitual tendencies (*xi*) are exhausted" (Part 4) states:

Regarding the phrase "the thirty-four minds where both the fundamental afflictions and habitual tendencies are exhausted," those who suddenly realize the stage of Arhat or Pratyekabuddha also attain it through the uninterrupted sequence of the thirty-four minds;
however, they do not exhaust both the fundamental afflictions and habitual tendencies all at once by means of these. As for the term "habitual tendencies" (*xi*), there is... [text continues]

There are the habits of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa-vāsanā*) as well as the habits of the sands of *dharmas* (*rajas-kaṣāya-vāsanā*). The Bodhisattva studies and practices the *dharmamukhas* as numerous as the sands of the Ganges to remedy his inferior wisdom.

Within each and every gate, he employs the contemplation of the Four Truths (*catur-āryasatya*) to subdue the active afflictions (*kleśa*). Within each and every gate, he practices the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) to permeate the habits of view and thought.
Therefore, through the thirty-four moments of mind beneath the tree, he realizes the Four Noble Truths upon the *dharmas* as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; thus, it causes—

Because they maintain both the fundamental afflictions (*kleśa*) and the two types of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) until their exhaustion, they are able to reach the ultimate realization of both truths.

Regarding the commentary on the *Avalokiteśvara-sūtra* explaining the Pratyekabuddha’s attenuation of habitual tendencies (the attenuation of habitual tendencies by a Pratyekabuddha is considered a shallow stage), Volume Thirteen:

In the cultivation of a Pratyekabuddha, no partial fruits are established. They deeply contemplate dependent origination and have long practiced the "three many" [generosities]. Since their merit and wisdom are already flourishing...

Anticipating the submergence of the two habits, although one has not yet manifested the Truth, the four currents cannot move them; this is called "attaining the shallow place. To suddenly realize the ultimate fruit is called "reaching the other shore."
In the *Miaozongchao* (Excerpts on the Wondrous Doctrine), the two instances concerning "love" (*āsvāda*) and "hatred" (*pratigha*) are both categorized among the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).

(7) Question: The *Śāstra* states that when Kāśyapa encountered the five superior and exquisite sensual desires of a bodhisattva, he was so overcome by love that he could not remain still and rose to dance.

Yet, in the *Lotus Sūtra*, Kāśyapa recounts that in the past he considered the bodhisattvas' teachings shallow; they wandered and transformed through supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), yet he did not give rise to even a single [affliction]. How is this to be understood?

One should reflect upon the mind that delights in [worldly] pleasures. Both of these matters are the dharmas of a bodhisattva; for what reason, then, do love and hatred suddenly become so diametrically opposed?
One should know that both minds are distinct afflictions (*paryavasthāna*). To love exquisite desires is the same as the "thinking of the same substance" (*tongti-si*);

to hate the saving of sentient beings is like the "dust-like sands" (*chena*) of the realms beyond. It is like not turning one's back on one's child, yet loving only wealth and status while neglecting the cultivation of their name. This serves as an analogy.

In the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, it rebukes Śāriputra, saying: "If habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are not yet exhausted, flowers will cling to the body. Because one fears birth and death, the five desires find an opportunity.
Since one already fears birth and death, one merely points to the 'dust-like sands' [of phenomena] as being these habitual tendencies."
The *Nyāyānusāra* indicates that non-defiled ignorance is also termed "habitual tendency" (*vāsanā*).
Thus, non-defiled ignorance is also called habitual tendency because it is a residual trace left by the repeated cultivation of afflictions; it is the "breath" of that habituation.

Only a Buddha has eternally severed this; as long as these two types of "breaths" remain, [the state] is not yet perfected. It is also termed "unwavering wisdom seeking liberation," or alternatively termed "erroneous [wisdom]."
Regarding "wisdom and so forth," it is not because their substance (*tattva*) is identical.

The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* clarifies that the "dust-sands" of the Small Vehicle's habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are themselves habitual tendencies; this refers to the repeated cultivation of inferior wisdom, which is unable to universally comprehend all objects and seeds. Furthermore...
It is said: "Non-defiled ignorance can obscure the true meaning of all flavors and so forth, thereby obstructing the true vision of all flavors and so forth.
